short.titel: Marlboro – PULLED FROM THE MARKET, THEN WORLD NO. 1
short.text:
Marlboro was briefly pulled from the market. So how did it reach number one worldwide?

It launched in 1924 as America's luxury cigarette, sold mainly in hotels and resorts.

Marketed to women, it stagnated below 1% of US tobacco sales before the war.

So what changed? After a 1950s lung cancer study, Philip Morris repositioned Marlboro for men.

Leo Burnett's agency dropped copy. The Marlboro Man was a sea captain, gunsmith, athlete, cowboy.

By 1972, the once-pulled brand was the world's best-selling tobacco brand.

lang.text:
One order crushed Broadcom's takeover of Qualcomm.

So what does a company do after a blow like that? But the real surprise came afterward.

This video answers one question: how did a blocked chip bid push Broadcom into software?

Broadcom proposed buying Qualcomm for 130 billion dollars in mid-November 2017. Qualcomm's board rebuffed it. The hostile takeover was later revised to 117 billion dollars.

Then the Trump administration blocked it with an executive order. The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States had concerns. Broadcom, then headquartered in Singapore, was considered too close to China and chipmaker Huawei.

The committee warned that Chinese dominance in 5G would have substantial negative national security consequences. Critics said competitiveness mattered more than security. Two days after the order, Broadcom withdrew.

Be sure to like, share and save this video.

The failed bid led Broadcom and its CEO to look at infrastructure software instead. That means programs companies use to run their computer systems.

But how does a chip company end up buying a cybersecurity giant? It started with an older kind of software.

CA Technologies was a longtime giant in mainframe software. It had expanded into cloud computing. News sources reported terms for 18.9 billion dollars in July 2018. Broadcom announced the completed deal on 5 November 2018.

Next came Symantec's enterprise security business, bought for 10.7 billion dollars in cash. Broadcom announced the completed deal on 4 November 2019, and the Symantec name and brand came along. The consumer software side is now Gen Digital.

Broadcom's share ranked fifth best among listed shares of the 2010s, with a total return of 1,956 percent as of 2019.

But how did a company get big enough to bid for Qualcomm at all?

It began inside Hewlett-Packard, as a semiconductor division called HP Associates. It left in the 1999 Agilent Technologies spinoff. KKR and Silver Lake paid 2.6 billion dollars for the unit in 2005, and formed Avago Technologies.

Avago traded pieces early on. It sold an I/O solutions unit to PMC-Sierra for 42.5 million dollars. Then it bought Infineon's Munich bulk acoustic wave business for 21.5 million euros.

Avago went public on NASDAQ on 6 August 2009 as AVGO. Then came the real shift. It agreed to buy LSI Corporation for 6.6 billion dollars in December 2013. That moved it away from specialized products, toward a more mainstream industry that included storage chips for data centers.

It also sold parts of what it bought. The SSD controller business went to Seagate in May 2014. LSI's Axxia networking business went to Intel for 650 million dollars. By August 2014, Avago was the ninth-largest semiconductor company.

Then came the giant. Avago announced a 37 billion dollar deal for Broadcom Corporation in May 2015. That was 17 billion dollars in cash and 20 billion in shares.

Here is the odd part. Avago was the nominal survivor, but the combined company would take the Broadcom name. It would have annual revenue of 15 billion dollars and a market value of 77 billion.

Broadcom Corporation also made the company the ninth largest patent holder among top semiconductor vendors, according to LexInnova. Cypress paid 550 million dollars in May 2016 for its Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and Zigbee IoT products.

Not every deal went smoothly. Broadcom proposed buying Brocade Communications Systems in 2016, a 5.5 billion dollar cash offer. The foreign investment committee delayed it for review.

Broadcom announced it would move its legal address from Singapore to Delaware on 2 November 2017. That would avoid the review. The move was linked to the parent being renamed Broadcom Inc. The old Broadcom Corporation stayed on as a wholly owned subsidiary.

Within weeks came the Qualcomm bid, and Broadcom was still headquartered in Singapore.

Then came the biggest software bet of all. Broadcom announced a deal for VMware, a virtualization and cloud computing software vendor, in May 2022. The deal was valued at 69 billion dollars, in cash and stock.

Regulators were not quick to agree. The UK regulator investigated whether the deal would substantially lessen competition. The European Commission investigated too. The completion date slipped from 26 May 2023 to as late as 26 November 2023.

China was the last hurdle. It approved the deal with conditions. VMware's server software had to work with local hardware and not restrict customers to Broadcom's hardware.

The deal closed on 22 November 2023. CEO Hock Tan announced the headquarters would move from San Jose to VMware's campus in Palo Alto.

Three months later, Broadcom sold the end-user computing division it inherited to KKR for 4 billion dollars. KKR had helped create Avago in 2005.

But did all that growth come with a price? Regulators had questions about how Broadcom treated customers.

Reports in January 2018 said the FTC had been investigating for several months. Broadcom agreed to settle in 2021. The FTC claimed it abused its monopoly power with restrictive contract terms and threats of retaliation against customers it deemed disloyal.

The European Commission ordered it to stop allegedly anticompetitive practices in October 2019. Commissioner Margrethe Vestager said terms with six main customers would create serious and irreversible harm to competition if no action were taken. Broadcom committed to suspend exclusivity or quasi-exclusivity agreements, and not to make such deals for seven years.

VMware drew complaints too. A European cloud trade group alleged in March 2026 that prices had risen tenfold since the acquisition. Broadcom denied the allegations, and the European Commission said it was assessing the complaint.

Broadcom also fought over patents. It sued smart TV makers in 2017, and the U.S. International Trade Commission ruled for the manufacturers. It sued Netflix in 2020. Critics argued it was suing Netflix for being more successful.

Today the mix looks different. As of 2025, 58 percent of revenue came from semiconductor products and 42 percent from infrastructure software.

Chips still matter. Raspberry Pi revealed in early 2020 that its new boards would use a Broadcom BCM2711 chip. Broadcom said in July 2026 that it extended its Apple partnership through 2031.

Broadcom passed 1 trillion dollars in market value in December 2024, the 12th company to do it. It passed 2 trillion dollars in April 2026.

So here's the answer. A national security order blocked the Qualcomm bid, and Broadcom withdrew two days later. The failed bid led Broadcom and its CEO to look at infrastructure software as another way to grow. CA Technologies came first, then Symantec's enterprise security business and VMware.

Hock Tan is president and CEO, and the company is headquartered in Palo Alto. The blocked bid didn't end Broadcom's growth. It sent that growth into software.
